items.note: Bhoj shifted his capital from Ujjain to Dhar for security, developed Dhara with rampart and moat, re-founded Ujjain and Vidisha, and founded Bhojpur.
Bhoj wrote the Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra, a vast treatise on town-architecture, and in practice founded cities, adorning Dhar and Ujjain with 84 crossroads each with a temple.
Paramāra founder born from Vasishtha's fire-pit and named Paramāra for driving off foes, per contemporary literary and epigraphic sources.
Upendra among early Paramāra kings; Siyaka (Śrīharṣa) the first with tenth-century copper-plate grants; his sons Vākpatirāja Muñja and Sindhurāja.
Muñja a king, poet and patron of Padmagupta, Dhananjaya, Dhanapāla, Amitagati and Halāyudha; Padmagupta composed the Navasāhasāṅka-carita.
Dating Bhoj: a text of 1055 shows him alive to 1055; ruling 55 years 7 months 3 days points to accession around 999 CE.
Many copper-plate grants and inscriptions of Bhoj exist; history and tradition complement each other for knowledge of him.
According to the Udaipur Praśasti, Bhoj defeated the Chedi king, Indraratha, Toggala, Bhima and the kings of Karṇāṭa, Lāṭa and Gurjara, and the Turuṣkas.
Bhoj's list of defeated kings and the title Mahārājādhirāja Parameśvara.
Muñja made Bhoj alone king as the most capable; other kinsmen were displeased but the kingdom remained with Bhoj.
Sanskrit verse in which Muñja (Vākpatirāja) himself consecrates Bhoj to the kingdom.
items.gloss: To him was born a son, Shri Bhoj, whose palms bore auspicious marks such as lotus, pitcher and parasol; Muñja, the abode of valour, out of affection and judging him worthy, himself consecrated him to the kingdom.

items.note: After Muñja's death Sindhurāja acted as regent for Bhoj; Bhoj took up governance around 999 CE.
Bhoj's court said to have five hundred poets and scholars, including Uchchata, Dhanapāla, Halāyudha, Amitagati and Chittapa; poetry recitation, debate and displays of art were held.
Bhoj built halls at Dhārā and Ujjayinī (Sharada-sadam, Bharati-bhavan, Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa) with poetry, treatises and grammar engraved on slabs and pillars.
Bhoj urged scholars to write treatises; Ubbaṭa, Dhanapāla, Chhittapa and Amitagati named; poet of the Shyāmalā-daṇḍaka given a hundred villages in 1001 CE.
Prabandha-chintāmaṇi gives Bhoj 104 compositions and epithets; a commentary on his Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa gives 84 works; Dhara had 84 crossroads and temples.
Bhoj as appreciator of merit and patron, himself poet, poetician and composer of treatises, with 104 song-compositions and 84 works.
Prabhāvaka-charita: Bhoj's works on many subjects, including architecture (vāstu), were read and taught at the Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa palace in Ujjain.
Bhoj had an image of Vāgdevī made in Samvat 1091 (1034 CE), now in the British Museum, and composed a hymn to her.
Bhoj's Śṛṅgāra-mañjarī-kathā, a cycle of thirteen stories, includes a description of Bhoj and of Dhārā.
Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra, an incomplete work of seven thousand verses, sets principles on architecture; Bhoj in practice founded Dhārā, Ujjain and Bhojpur and built temples, tanks and dams.
Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa on poetics: five chapters, with 24 varieties each of word, sense and combined figures, and new figures discussed.
Of Bhoj's philosophical works the Tattva-prakāśa is most famous; commentaries began in the twelfth century; it is a work on Śaiva philosophy held in regard in its tradition.
Bhoj became hero of tales in his lifetime; stories appear in Siṃhāsana-dvātriṃśikā and an ancient Mongolian-language book.
Bhoj's synthesis of contemporary religions: listen to the Buddhists, act as the Jains, conduct oneself as the Vedics, and meditate upon Lord Śiva.
Sanskrit verse attributed to Bhoj, ending with meditation on the Supreme Śiva, with the author's English rendering.
items.gloss: The Buddha's doctrine should be heard; that of the Jain should be practised; the Vedic should be followed in conduct; the Supreme Śiva should be meditated upon.

items.note: Bhoj founded Dharanagari, Ujjayinī, Vidisha (Bhaillasvāmipur, later Bhelsa), Bhojpur (Raisen) and Bhojpur near Patna; shifted his capital from Ujjayinī to Dhārā.
Bhoj had temples in the Bhūmija style built in his kingdom.

claim.value: Bhoj had Bhūmija temples built in his kingdom

items.note: Bhoj built Bhūmija-style temples of Kedāra, Rāmeśvara, Somanātha, Muṇḍira and Mahākāla as pañcāyatana complexes, plus the Bhojpur temple and the Tribhuvananārāyaṇa temple at Chittaur.

claim.value: Bhūmija temples as pañcāyatana complexes of Bhoj's period

items.note: The dam Bhoj built on the Betwa at Bhojpur near Bhopal formed a lake of 250 square miles, demolished by Hoshang Shah of Mandu; its remnant is said to be Bhopal's lake.
Bhojśālā at Dhar, one of Bhoj's Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa halls, carries abundant stone-inscribed literature; a stone-inscribed library.
Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra, in the tradition of the Mayamata and Mānasāra, is devoted to architecture, covering towns, palaces, temples, sculpture and painting.
Paramāra kings patronised architecture; constructions or remains of Muñja, Bhoj, Udayāditya and Devapāladeva are found here and there.
Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra is the work with detailed guiding instructions for the architect, up to the roof ('samarāṅgaṇa').
Patañjali's residence Gonarda identified as Godarmau near Bhopal; Buddhist literature shows it as a trading centre between Vidisha and Ujjayinī.
Countless mentions of Ujjayinī and Vidisha in Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, Buddhist and Jain literature; a systematic description first in Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Kādambarī.

items.note: Per the Samarāṅgaṇa-sūtradhāra, vāstu is the dwelling-ground built of brick, stone, wood and iron; village, town and fort are built under this craft.
Town-planning prescriptions: choose a delightful region, test the soil, and only then lay out village, town and pattana.

items.note: The enclosing wall (vapra) is stated to be of five kinds: square, oblong, circular, circular-oblong and fully round (Sa.Su. verse).
items.gloss: Square, oblong, circular, again circular-oblong, and fully round: of these, the forms of the rampart are only five.

items.note: Prescription for a capital: four gate-passages, a gopura, an enclosing wall, markets, temples, an earthen rampart with a moat, and a royal residence.
